unit_label: CB Module E unit 1: evolution of regulation and supervision (courseware unit 13)

facts.statement: Theoretical underpinnings (courseware): central bank regulation and supervision over the commercial banks and financial institutions is a somewhat recent phenomenon; the need for regulation and supervision arises on account of the importance of banks in managing finance flows; the alternative systems in vogue regarding regulation and supervision globally are examined with reference to the pros and cons of separating the regulatory and supervisory role from Central Bank and the feasibility of assigning the latter role to a separate agency like the erstwhile Financial Services Authority (FSA) of the U.K.; the recent reversal of this move by UK in terms of which the supervisory role was brought within the ambit of the Bank of England to a large extent corroborated the view that the central banks are best equipped in performing this role rather than any other agency. Genesis: the conduct of supervision to single out banks as a special category of institution requiring the attentions of a supervisor implies no special lack of confidence in the capacity of bankers to manage their own affairs; rather, it arises from the unique fiduciary responsibility which bankers assume when they accept other peoples money for safe keeping; that is why when introducing legislation, several countries took the view that the important activity which would be the trigger for statutory control was the act of deposit taking. But in addition to this micro-level concern for the interests of individual depositors, there is also a macroeconomic dimension which needs to be constantly in the supervisors view; banks have a central intermediary role in sustaining economic activity, and the maintenance of a sound banking system is essential for the fruitful development of both the national and the international economy; supervision has evolved and grown in most advanced economies voluntarily and out of the market; while it has always been a feature of the Banks approach to supervision to sail with a light rudder, it is always necessary to be mindful of the Charybdis of prudential laxity across the channel from the Scylla of overbearing regulation. In UK, the extent of the banks supervision has grown over the past decades in two directions: triggered by the secondary banking crisis alongside EEC developments, the first one has been the widening of the Banks supervision to include institutions not traditionally under its control; these developments called for appropriate statutory backing; the second has been the stretching of the banks supervisory horizons to embrace in a more comprehensive way the totality of banks operations spread over different regions and countries; the widening of the Banks role was given added momentum, as for example, with the passage of banking legislation in 1979 in UK; the Banking Act of that year invested the Bank for the first time with a statutory responsibility for the supervision of deposit-taking institutions. Co-operation between supervisory authorities: in recent years, the international dimension of supervision has developed alongside the growing international character of banks operations; the expansion of a bank beyond national frontiers poses immediate supervisory problems. The primary focus on the CAMELS parameters: capital adequacy, management quality, earnings (or profitability) and liquidity, abbreviated as the CAMEL; the missing item is Asset quality; the supervisors check list; it is generally, far from exclusively, the case that most of the losses incurred by banks arise from their lending. Supervisor and auditor: the success of supervision depends on the relationship between the supervisor and the bank auditor; the auditor task is to report on the information presented by directors in the company accounts and to give an opinion to shareholders; the supervisor primary responsibility is to a banks depositors; the depositor merits a more active protection, and the supervisor has thus not only to form his own judgement of a bank condition but also to undertake whatever action appears necessary to protect depositors interests; the auditor concerned primarily with establishing the truth of facts presented to him by management and the appropriateness of the judgments made in relation to those facts, while the supervisor concern extends to the implication of those facts and judgments for the future viability of the business; this reflects the different character of the obligations to shareholders and depositors.

Global backdrop (courseware): the history of central banks contributing to financial stability was one of their roles in most countries; even when central banks were assigned a relatively narrow mandate, such as that of inflation targeting in recent years, they often played a decisive part as soon as financial instability struck; their ability to act as lender of last resort in the financial system and to manage liquidity in the interbank market typically made them a key player in crisis management; in times of crisis, the central bank through the lender-of-last-resort interventions endeavours to restore or maintain financial stability; but central banks were not always and everywhere tasked with banking supervision, which varies from country to country; in the late 1990s there was a trend for supervision to be placed outside central banks and entrusted to cross-sectoral authorities in charge of banks, insurance and securities industries. United Kingdom: there was no formal system of banking regulation and no agency was empowered by law to deal with banking problems until the 1970s, except the provisions of the Companies Act; many banks collapsed during the early nineteenth century; the spiralling bank failures forced the government to permit by law from 1826 the formation of joint stock banks including the right to spread among numerous proprietors; in 1866, the spectacular collapse of bill brokers - Overend Gurney and Company and in 1878 the collapse of the City of Glasgow Bank; in 1890, the Bank of England helped the banking system recover from the crash of Baring Brothers, a leading merchant banking house in London, which was rescued by a guarantee fund of over pound 17 million promised; the crisis was averted but the leading role played by the BoE demonstrated the responsibility it had to carry for the stability of the banking system; in the 1970s, the secondary banking crisis (late 1973) triggered by high interest rates caused the collapse of many of these banks from funding the diversification of the larger banks; the Bank of England launched a rescue operation supported by the clearing banks; the result was the Banking Act, 1976, which increased the formal role of BoE in supervision and regulation of the banking system. United States: only State Governments had the power to regulate banks and this consisted mainly in issuing bank charters; in 1863 the Federal Government began to take active interest in bank regulation; the National Bank Act of 1864 provided that a Federal Agency, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, would have the power to license banks; the Federal Reserve Act of 1913 (Owen-Glass Act) created the Federal Reserve System, which functioned primarily as a holding institution for reserves and as a money-creator of last resort to prevent the downward spiral of withdrawal of funds. The Great Depression: in the early 1930s the economic depression had a disastrous impact on the banking system; many banks found it difficult to continue; by the beginning of 1933 the American people were starting to lose faith in their banking system; when Franklin D. Roosevelt was elected as president, he declared a four-day bank holiday (March 9, 1933 Congress passed the Emergency Banking Relief Act); the Banking Act, 1933 was later enacted: the Federal Reserve Board was given tighter control of the investment practices of banks and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation was set up to insure all deposits in banks up to US$ 5,000. Canada: the Canadian Government established the Office of the Inspector General of Banks in 1925 after the collapse of the Home Bank; the Bank of Canada was created nine years later (1934); the experience in some other countries (Chile, Mexico, Peru, the Scandinavian countries) developed central banks and bank regulators completely separately; more recently, countries such as the UK and Australia have modified the institutional mandates of their central banks by transferring their regulatory responsibilities to a separate agency; the experiences of countries in creating an appropriate structure and entrusting the responsibility of bank regulation and supervision vary considerably, although the basic motive has been to maintain systemic stability; there is a considerable cross-national variation in the institutional structure of financial regulation and supervision, and the legislation related to it.

Interactions between monetary policy and supervision and integration versus separation (courseware): benefits of integration: a bank supervisory role could offer benefits to monetary policy, particularly in terms of informational advantages; it has been argued that by integration of the supervision function with the central bank, creates new opportunities for the conduct of monetary policy and other functions closely related to it; four areas: the state of the macro-economy; monetary policy options; interactions with supervisory policies; and the management of the central bank balance sheet; the opportunities are greater in turbulent times than in quiet times. Data collected and analysed as part of banking supervision provide valuable additional information about the banking sector and may feed into the assessment of the macroeconomic situation; additional supervisory data and analyses, be they micro-prudential or macro-prudential, would further enhance the breadth, depth, and granularity of information about the functioning of the economy; the value added of this information will become even more critical in a crisis; an analytical supervisory assessment and early-warning tools can put the new data to work in assessing credit developments; a key feature in crisis is the impairment of the monetary transmission mechanism in which fragilities in banks funding models and their exposure to NPAs play a significant role; an understanding of banks behaviour and health across jurisdictions facilitates the design and implementation of non-standard monetary policy measures. Conflicts of interest: the literature on whether adding banking supervision to monetary policy creates conflicts of interest is not well developed; the concern is that a central bank which is in charge of supervision would turn into a supervisor with access to central bank liquidity; Stefan Gerlach: it could then occasionally relax its monetary policy, potentially generating an inflationary bias impairing its credibility and contribute to more risk-taking by banks (moral hazard) and in turn breed future financial instability; the central bank could be inclined to continue lending to weak banks for fear that winding them up would trigger losses; conflict between monetary policy objectives and prudential goals arises particularly in conditions of serious economic or financial system stress; for example when inflationary pressures require interest rates to be raised sharply and banks are potentially exposed to possible write-downs of their asset valuations; another issue that could arise would be if the central bank became deeply involved in managing a banking crisis; monetary policy interacts with supervisory and regulatory policies, be they micro-prudential or macro-prudential in nature: if the monetary policy objective and the supervisory objective are distinctly defined and separate instruments are assigned to each of them, then a single institution could take the interdependencies better into account than separate authorities; research confirms that it is advisable for monetary policy to focus on price stability and prudential policy on financial stability; against this background, as an institution with a clear price stability mandate, compliance with which can be easily verified, the central bank will have incentives to intensify the prudential policies seeking to counteract emerging financial imbalances and risks; efforts have been made to resolve the conflicts of interests: for example, the regulation proposed by the European Commission called for a governance structure that strictly separates the monetary functions from the supervisory functions: separation of the decision-making bodies which should also include distinct objectives for these bodies and different policy instruments. Integration vs separation: while the importance of central bank independence for the conduct of monetary policy has been the subject matter of numerous empirical studies, relatively little research has been focused on the significance of other aspects of the structure of the central bank, particularly its role in bank supervision; roughly three-quarters of OECD nations assign their central banks either sole or shared responsibility for bank supervision; many of these countries are reviewing those responsibilities; for example, in mid-1997 the Bank of England was given greater independence but was relieved of its bank supervisory responsibilities; the former Governor of the Bank of England had said that monetary and financial stability are interrelated; the former US Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan stated that the Federal Reserve Board believes that financial modernization should not undermine the ability and authority of the central bank to manage crises, ensure an efficient and safe payment system, and conduct monetary policy; the former Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke opined that modernization of the banking system and the improvement of bank regulation and supervision are essential for promoting stable monetary policy and low inflation; Professor Charles Goodhart: after all, banking supervisors and those in the central bank concerned with systemic stability must continue to work closely together wherever the supervisors are physically located.

Genesis of bank regulation and supervision in India and the Indian perspective (courseware): indigenous systems of banking existed in India for centuries; the roots of commercial banking in India date to early eighteenth century (Box 13.1): the East India Company set up Bank of Bombay in 1720; in 1773 Warren Hastings floated the General Bank of Bengal and Bihar, which was a private establishment but under the patronage of East India Company Government; in 1786 the General Bank of India was floated; the first Presidency Bank: Bank of Calcutta (1806) became Bank of Bengal (1809), the Bank of Bombay (1840) and Bank of Madras (1843); Government bank started functioning in Madras (1806) by the resolution of Bentinck; Presidency Banks could issue notes subject to certain restrictions; the Paper Currency Act, 1861 brought the right to issue notes by Presidency banks to an end and entrusted to the Government; in 1876 the Presidency Bank Act came into existence, which brought the three Presidency banks under the common statute and restriction on business; the Imperial Bank of India was formed in 1921 by amalgamating the three Presidency Banks; in 1951 when the first Five Year Plan was launched, the development of rural India was accorded the highest priority; the All India Rural Credit Survey Committee recommended the creation of a State partnered and State-sponsored bank by taking over the Imperial Bank of India and integrating with it the former State-owned or State-associated banks; the State Bank of India Act was passed in May 1955 and the SBI was constituted on 1 July 1955; State Bank of India (Subsidiary Banks) Act was passed in 1959; Bharatiya Mahila Bank and the associate banks (SBBJ, SBH, SBM, SBP, SBT) merged with SBI with effect from April 1, 2017. In the initial and formative stage of commercial banking development in India the banks were regulated and governed by the East India Company Government (following the Royal Charter) and the Government; the law relating to banking companies were contained in the Indian Companies Act; company law was introduced in India with the Companies Act of 1850, which was based on the English Companies Act, 1844; in 1857 an Act for the incorporation and regulation of joint stock companies; the privilege of limited liability was not extended to banks under the English Companies Act of 1857; the law relating to companies was re-enacted in the Companies Act, 1913, which was made applicable to banking companies as well. A banking crisis that occurred during 1913 revealed weaknesses of the banking system such as the maintenance of an unduly low proportion of cash and other liquid assets, the grant of large unsecured advances to directors of banks and to the companies in which the directors were interested; some banks had expanded rapidly and later collapsed; in West Bengal four scheduled banks and many non-scheduled banks failed; the Indian Central Banking Enquiry Committee (1929-31) was set up with terms of reference including the banking with a view to protecting the interest of the public; the Committee emphasised the need for enacting a special Bank Act covering the organisation, management, audit and liquidation of banks. The efforts towards reviving the banking system through the passage of a more comprehensive Banking Act were made in September-October 1943; on April, 1945 the Finance Member moved in the Legislative Assembly a motion for reference of the Bill to a Select Committee; the Banking Companies (Inspection) Ordinance, 1946 and the Banking Companies (Restriction of Branches) Act, 1946 were passed as interim measures; the Banking Companies Act, 1949 was passed on February 1949 (the Banking Regulation Act from 1966); the Department of Banking Operations of the Reserve Bank, which was entrusted with the administration of the Act, was originally organised in August 1945 to provide the requisite administrative machinery. The conduct of monetary policy and compatibility with regulatory and supervisory role (the Indian perspective): an important debate is whether there is any inherent conflict in discharging both the monetary policy and supervisory functions simultaneously by the central bank; an important argument for preserving a financial stability function in a central bank, even when regulation of financial entities is carried out by another institution, is that monetary policy and financial stability policies are intertwined; financial sector stability is best achieved in the context of a stable macroeconomic environment; international experience shows that financial and banking distress has been inextricably linked to currency and macroeconomic crises; therefore prudential policies need to aim at promoting the financial system resilience; there is a two-way interrelationship between monetary policy and banking soundness; the banking system continues to be the main vehicle for monetary policy signals in a country; bank soundness should be a legitimate concern of the central bank. In India the supervisory activities of the Reserve Bank have benefited from its price stability objective, and it is widely recognised that safety and soundness of banks must be pursued jointly with its responsibility for promoting stability and growth in the economy; the Reserve Bank has the responsibilities for monetary policy and supervision; to carry out its overall responsibilities, the Reserve Bank has to develop extensive and detailed knowledge of the intricacies of both Indian and global financial systems; supervision tools are less blunt; the ability to manage crises and, more importantly, to avoid them; it is conceded that the Reserve Bank ability to respond expeditiously to any particular financial stress does not necessitate comprehensive information on each banking institution; the supervisory responsibilities give important qualitative and quantitative information on how its policy stance is affecting bank actions; the rising shares of bank credit to housing, real estate and retail finances will warrant appropriate policy responses to ensure credit quality; asset price changes can have a powerful effect on investment and consumption through a financial accelerator effect; large swings in asset price changes pose a challenge for monetary policy from the regulatory and supervisory perspective; the Reserve Bank increased the risk weight, in December 2004, on loans in case of housing loans from 50 per cent to 75 per cent and in case of consumer credit including personal loans and credit cards from 100 per cent to 125 per cent; subsequently the risk weight for credit risk on capital market and commercial real estate exposures were increased from 100 per cent to 125 per cent in July 2005; confidential supervisory information garnered through bank examinations can potentially improve the conduct of monetary policy; therefore, it is advantageous to simultaneously pursue the monetary policy function along with banking regulation and supervision; in the Indian context, these two functions are more complementary than conflicting.

payload.title: Why banks are supervised and what supervision does
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Why banks:** supervision of banks arises from the **fiduciary responsibility** bankers accept when they take **other people's money for safekeeping**, not from doubts about bankers' ability. The act of **deposit taking** is the usual **trigger for statutory control**. There is also a **macroeconomic** concern: banks have a **central intermediary role** and a **sound banking system** is essential to national and international economies.

**Style:** supervision has grown in advanced economies **voluntarily and out of the market**; the supervisor must avoid both **prudential laxity** and **overbearing regulation** ('Scylla and Charybdis').

**UK growth:** after the **secondary banking crisis**, the Bank of England's supervision **widened to institutions not previously under its control** and **stretched across regions and countries**; the **Banking Act 1979** gave it **statutory responsibility** for supervising **deposit-taking institutions** (the courseware also links the formal role to the **Banking Act 1976**).

**International dimension:** banks beyond national borders require **co-operation between supervisors**.

**CAMEL(S):** supervisors examine **Capital adequacy, Management quality, Earnings and Liquidity** (the **missing item is Asset quality**, since **most bank losses arise from lending**).

**Supervisor vs auditor:** the **auditor reports to shareholders** on the **truth of the accounts**; the **supervisor's primary responsibility is to depositors**, so the supervisor must **form his own judgement** and take **action to protect depositors**, looking at **future viability**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Supervisors protect depositors and system stability, which goes beyond the auditor role.

self_check.prompt_text: To whom is the supervisor primarily responsible, in contrast with the auditor?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The bank's depositors (the auditor reports to shareholders).

payload.title: Global backdrop: the UK, the US, the Great Depression and Canada
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Central banks and stability:** even with narrow mandates, central banks act as **lender of last resort** and manage **interbank liquidity**, so they are **key crisis managers**; but **supervision is not always placed in the central bank**: from the **late 1990s** some countries moved it to **cross-sector authorities**.

**United Kingdom:** no formal banking regulation until the **1970s** except the **Companies Act**; **joint stock banks were allowed from 1826** after repeated failures; **1866 Overend Gurney** and **1878 City of Glasgow Bank** failures; **1890 Baring Brothers**: the **Bank of England** organised a **guarantee fund of over GBP 17 million** to avert crisis, showing its **responsibility for stability**; the **secondary banking crisis (from 1973)** led to a Bank of England **rescue with the clearing banks** and the **Banking Act, 1976**, which raised its **formal supervisory role**.

**United States:** only **State governments** chartered banks until **1863**; the **National Bank Act 1864** created the **Office of the Comptroller of the Currency** to **license banks**; there was **no central bank from 1836 to 1914**; the **Federal Reserve Act 1913 (Owen-Glass)** created the Federal Reserve as a **reserve holder and money-creator of last resort**.

**Great Depression:** by **1933** faith in banks had collapsed; **President Roosevelt** declared a **four-day bank holiday** and the **Emergency Banking Relief Act (9 March 1933)** followed; the **Banking Act 1933** tightened Federal Reserve control and set up the **Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation** to insure deposits **up to US$ 5,000**.

**Canada:** the **Inspector General of Banks (1925)** was created after the **Home Bank** collapse, **nine years before the Bank of Canada (1934)**. **Chile, Mexico, Peru and Scandinavia** developed **central banks and regulators separately**; the **UK and Australia** later **moved regulation to a separate agency**. Structures vary widely but all aim at **systemic stability**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Crises, not design, drove most national regulatory structures.

self_check.prompt_text: Which US Act of 1864 gave the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency the power to license banks?

payload.title: Monetary policy and supervision: benefits, conflicts and integration versus separation
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Benefits of integration:** supervision gives the central bank **information** about the **macroeconomy**, **monetary policy options**, **interactions with supervisory policies** and **its own balance sheet**; the value is **greatest in turbulent times**. Supervisory data and **early-warning tools** reveal **credit developments** and show where **monetary transmission is impaired** by weak banks (funding fragilities, NPAs).

**Possible conflicts of interest:** a central bank that supervises banks and also **provides liquidity** may **relax monetary policy** (**inflationary bias**) or **lend to weak banks** (**moral hazard**) for fear that **closing them would cause losses**; in **stress**, **raising interest rates** to fight inflation can threaten **banks' asset values**; managing a **banking crisis** can **divert** attention. (**Stefan Gerlach**).

**Resolution:** research suggests monetary policy should focus on **price stability** and prudential policy on **financial stability**; with **separate objectives and instruments**, a **single institution** can use the **interdependence**; the **European Commission** proposed a governance structure that **strictly separates** monetary and supervisory **decision-making bodies**, with **distinct objectives and instruments**.

**Integration vs separation:** about **three-quarters of OECD countries** give central banks **sole or shared supervision**; the **Bank of England** was **relieved of supervision in mid-1997** when given greater independence; the **Fed** (Greenspan, Bernanke) argues it **needs supervision** to manage crises, ensure payments safety and conduct monetary policy; **Goodhart:** supervisors and central bank staff on systemic stability must **work closely together wherever the supervisors sit**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The debate weighs information gains against the risk of lenient monetary or prudential policy.

self_check.prompt_text: What risk does Stefan Gerlach identify when a central bank with access to liquidity also supervises banks?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It may relax monetary policy (inflationary bias) and encourage bank risk-taking (moral hazard), including lending to weak banks.

payload.title: Genesis of bank regulation and supervision in India and the Indian perspective
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Early banking (Box 13.1):** the **East India Company** set up the **Bank of Bombay (1720)**; **Warren Hastings** floated the **General Bank of Bengal and Bihar (1773)**; the **General Bank of India (1786)**. The **Presidency Banks**: **Bank of Calcutta (1806)** → **Bank of Bengal (1809)**, **Bank of Bombay (1840)**, **Bank of Madras (1843)**; the **Paper Currency Act, 1861** ended their note issue; the **Presidency Banks Act 1876** put them under one law; the **Imperial Bank of India (1921)** merged them; after the **All India Rural Credit Survey** the **SBI Act (May 1955)** created the **State Bank of India (1 July 1955)**; the **1959 Subsidiary Banks Act** added associates, and the **associate banks and Bharatiya Mahila Bank merged with SBI from 1 April 2017**.

**Early law:** banking was governed by the **Companies Acts** (**1850**, **1857**, **1913**); **limited liability** for banks came later. The **1913 crisis** exposed **low cash ratios** and **large unsecured advances to directors**; the **Indian Central Banking Enquiry Committee (1929-31)** urged a **special Bank Act**; interim measures were the **Banking Companies (Inspection) Ordinance and (Restriction of Branches) Act, 1946**; the **Banking Companies Act, 1949** (later the **Banking Regulation Act, 1966**) followed; the **Department of Banking Operations** of the Reserve Bank (organised **August 1945**) administered it.

**Monetary policy and supervision in India:** financial stability is intertwined with **macroeconomic stability**; **banking distress and currency crises are linked**; banks are the **main vehicle of monetary policy signals**. Supervision gives the Reserve Bank **information** on how its policy affects banks and helps **calibrated tools**. Example: in **December 2004** the **risk weight on housing loans rose from 50 to 75 per cent** and on **consumer credit from 100 to 125 per cent**; in **July 2005** capital market and commercial real estate exposures rose **from 100 to 125 per cent**. The courseware concludes that in India monetary policy and supervision are **complementary rather than conflicting**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Banking legislation in India followed crises and the work of expert committees.
